title: What is Next.js?
description: Next.js is a React framework for building full-stack web applications.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Next.js is an open-source React framework maintained by Vercel. It adds what React leaves out: routing, data fetching, server rendering, caching, image and font optimization, and a build system (Turbopack).

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: Building a production React app requires many decisions and tools. Next.js gives you sensible defaults so you can focus on features, and lets each route choose how it renders: static, dynamic or streamed.

sections.title: Key ideas
sections.content:
- **App Router** (`app/` directory) built on React Server Components.
- Files define routes; special files (`page`, `layout`, `loading`, `error`) define UI.
- Server Functions and Route Handlers for backend logic.

codeExamples.title: A minimal page
codeExamples.explanation: A file named `page.tsx` inside `app/` becomes the `/` route. It's a Server Component by default.

commonMistakes: Thinking Next.js replaces React — it's built on React.
Assuming every page must be server-rendered on each request.
realWorldExample: Netflix Jobs, TikTok, Notion's marketing site and many SaaS dashboards are built with Next.js.
interviewTip: Describe it as 'a full-stack React framework' and name 3 capabilities: routing, rendering strategies, data/caching.

quiz.prompt: Next.js is best described as…
options: A React framework for full-stack web apps
quiz.explanation: It's a framework built on top of React.

title: Why Next.js?
description: The problems Next.js solves compared with a plain client-side React app.

sections.title: Problems with client-only SPAs
sections.content: A plain SPA sends an almost empty HTML file and builds the page in the browser. That can hurt SEO, slow the first meaningful paint, and push all data fetching to the client.

sections.title: What Next.js adds
sections.content:
- Pre-rendered HTML (static or per request) for fast loads and SEO.
- Server Components that keep code and secrets on the server.
- Automatic code splitting per route, prefetching links.
- `next/image`, `next/font`, metadata APIs.
- Backend code (Server Actions, Route Handlers) next to the UI.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.content: More concepts to learn (caching, server/client boundaries), and a server or platform to run dynamic features.

codeExamples.title: Same route, server data
codeExamples.explanation: The HTML arrives with the posts already in it — good for SEO and first paint. No loading spinner or client fetch needed.

commonMistakes: Choosing Next.js for an internal tool behind login where SEO doesn't matter, without considering simpler options.
Ignoring the operational cost of running a server.
realWorldExample: Marketing sites, e-commerce and content platforms rely on Next.js for SEO and fast first loads.
interviewTip: Give a balanced answer: benefits plus trade-offs.

quiz.prompt: A client-only SPA sends fully rendered HTML for each page by default.
quiz.explanation: It usually sends a near-empty HTML shell rendered by JavaScript in the browser.

flashcards.back: Pre-rendered HTML that crawlers can read immediately.

title: Project Structure
description: Create a Next.js app and understand its folders and special files.

sections.title: Getting started
sections.content: Run `npx create-next-app@latest`. Next.js 16 uses Turbopack by default and requires Node.js 20.9+.

sections.title: Top-level folders
sections.content:
- `app/` — routes, layouts and UI (App Router).
- `public/` — static files served from `/`.
- `src/` — optional wrapper for `app/`.
- `next.config.ts` — framework configuration.

sections.title: Special files in app/
sections.content:
- `layout` — shared UI wrapping child routes (the root layout is required).
- `page` — makes a route publicly accessible.
- `loading` — Suspense fallback; `error` — error boundary; `not-found` — 404 UI.
- `route` — API endpoint (Route Handler); `template` — re-mounted layout.
- `default` — fallback for parallel routes.

codeExamples.title: A typical tree
codeExamples.code:
app/
  layout.tsx          # root layout (html, body)
  page.tsx            # /
  blog/
    page.tsx          # /blog
    [slug]/
      page.tsx        # /blog/:slug
  api/
    health/route.ts   # GET /api/health
public/
  logo.svg            # /logo.svg
codeExamples.explanation: Folders create URL segments; `page` and `route` files make them reachable.

commonMistakes: Putting `page.tsx` and `route.ts` in the same folder (not allowed).
Forgetting that a folder without `page` isn't a route.
realWorldExample: Teams colocate components inside route folders using private folders like `_components`.
interviewTip: Name the special files and what each does.

quiz.prompt: Which file makes a folder publicly routable?
quiz.explanation: A route is only accessible when it has a page (or route) file.

flashcards.back: The root layout in app/, with <html> and <body>.

title: Pages Router (Overview)
description: The original Next.js router — still supported, but the App Router is recommended for new work.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Before Next.js 13, routes lived in `pages/`. Each file exported a React component, and data was loaded with special functions.

sections.title: Data functions
sections.content:
- `getStaticProps` — fetch at build time (SSG), optionally with `revalidate` (ISR).
- `getStaticPaths` — list dynamic paths to pre-render.
- `getServerSideProps` — fetch on every request (SSR).
- API routes in `pages/api`.

sections.title: App Router vs Pages Router
sections.content: The App Router adds Server Components, nested layouts, streaming, Server Actions and the new caching model. Both routers can coexist in one project during migration. The Pages Router is still supported but new features land in the App Router.

codeExamples.title: Pages Router data fetching
codeExamples.explanation: Data loads on each request and is passed as props. In the App Router, the page itself would be an async Server Component.

commonMistakes: Mixing `getServerSideProps` into App Router files — it only works in `pages/`.
Assuming you must migrate everything at once.
realWorldExample: Many large production apps still run on the Pages Router and migrate route by route.
interviewTip: Interviewers ask about both routers; know the mapping: getServerSideProps → dynamic Server Component, getStaticProps → cached/static Server Component.

quiz.prompt: getServerSideProps works inside the app/ directory.
quiz.explanation: It's a Pages Router API only.

title: The App Router
description: Next.js's file-system router built on React Server Components, layouts and streaming.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: The App Router uses the `app/` directory. Folders map to URL segments, and special files define UI for each segment. It's built on React's latest features: Server Components, Suspense, transitions and Actions.

sections.title: Why use it?
sections.content:
- Layouts that persist across navigations without re-rendering.
- Server Components by default → less client JavaScript.
- Built-in loading and error states per segment.
- Streaming and fine-grained caching.

sections.title: Component hierarchy
sections.content: For each segment Next.js nests: `layout` → `template` → `error` boundary → `loading` (Suspense) → `not-found` boundary → `page`.

codeExamples.title: Nested routes and layouts
codeExamples.explanation: Visiting `/dashboard/settings` renders the settings page inside the dashboard layout, inside the root layout. Navigating between dashboard pages keeps the sidebar mounted.

commonMistakes: Adding 'use client' to layouts unnecessarily.
Expecting layouts to re-render on every navigation.
realWorldExample: SaaS dashboards use nested layouts for sidebars and tabs that stay mounted across pages.
interviewTip: Explain the special-file hierarchy and server-first default.

quiz.prompt: Order the wrappers Next.js renders for a segment (outer → inner):
quiz.explanation: Layout wraps template, which wraps error, loading and finally the page.

flashcards.front: Do layouts re-render on navigation between their child pages?
flashcards.back: No, they preserve state and stay mounted.

title: File-based Routing
description: Folders become URL segments; special files make them render.

sections.title: How it works
sections.content:
- `app/page.tsx` → `/`
- `app/about/page.tsx` → `/about`
- `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` → `/blog/anything`

sections.title: Colocation
sections.content: Only `page` and `route` files are public, so you can safely keep components, tests and styles inside route folders. Prefix a folder with `_` (private folder) to exclude it from routing entirely.

sections.title: Organizing without changing URLs
sections.content: Folders in parentheses — route groups like `(marketing)` — organize files or share a layout without adding a URL segment.

codeExamples.title: Mapping files to URLs
codeExamples.code:
app/page.tsx                      ->  /
app/pricing/page.tsx              ->  /pricing
app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx    ->  /about
app/shop/[category]/page.tsx      ->  /shop/shoes
app/docs/[...slug]/page.tsx       ->  /docs/a/b/c
app/_components/Button.tsx        ->  (not routable)
codeExamples.explanation: Route groups and private folders help organize code; dynamic segments in brackets capture URL parts.

commonMistakes: Expecting a component file inside a route folder to be routable.
Creating two route groups that resolve to the same URL (build error).
realWorldExample: Marketing and app sections often live in `(marketing)` and `(app)` groups with different root layouts.
interviewTip: Explain colocation: only page/route files are public.

quiz.prompt: What URL does app/(shop)/cart/page.tsx serve?
quiz.explanation: Route groups are omitted from the URL.

flashcards.front: How to exclude a folder from routing?

title: The Link Component
description: Client-side navigation with automatic prefetching.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `<Link href="/about">` from `next/link` extends `<a>` with client-side navigation: only the changed segments are fetched and rendered, layouts persist, and state is preserved.

sections.title: Prefetching
sections.content: In production, links in the viewport are prefetched automatically. For static routes the whole route is prefetched; for dynamic routes, down to the nearest `loading.js` boundary. Use `prefetch={false}` for rarely used links.

sections.title: Tips
sections.content:
- Use Link for internal navigation, plain `<a>` for external URLs.
- Highlight the active link with `usePathname()` in a Client Component.

codeExamples.title: Active navigation link
codeExamples.explanation: `usePathname` reads the current path so the link can style itself and set `aria-current` for screen readers.

commonMistakes: Using `<a href>` for internal links, causing full page reloads.
Expecting prefetching to happen in development (it's production behaviour).
realWorldExample: E-commerce category menus prefetch product listing pages so navigation feels instant.
interviewTip: Mention soft navigation, prefetching and preserved layouts.

quiz.prompt: Links in the viewport are automatically prefetched in production.
quiz.explanation: Next.js prefetches visible links by default.

title: Programmatic Navigation
description: Navigate with useRouter, redirect and permanentRedirect.

sections.title: Client-side
sections.content: In Client Components, `useRouter()` from **`next/navigation`** (not `next/router`) gives `push`, `replace`, `back`, `forward`, `prefetch` and `refresh`. `router.refresh()` re-fetches Server Components for the current route without losing client state.

sections.title: Server-side
sections.content: In Server Components, Server Actions and Route Handlers, call `redirect('/login')` or `permanentRedirect('/new')` from `next/navigation`. They throw a special error to stop rendering, so don't wrap them in try/catch.

sections.title: Reading the URL
sections.content: `usePathname()`, `useSearchParams()` and `useParams()` in Client Components. Pages receive `params` and `searchParams` as **promises** (Next.js 15+).

codeExamples.title: Redirect after a mutation
codeExamples.explanation: After saving, the action revalidates the list and redirects to the new post.

commonMistakes: Importing useRouter from 'next/router' in the App Router.
Calling redirect() inside a try block, which swallows the redirect.
realWorldExample: Checkout flows redirect to a confirmation page from a Server Action after payment.
interviewTip: Know which import to use in each router and that redirect throws.

quiz.prompt: Where should useRouter be imported from in the App Router?
quiz.explanation: next/navigation is the App Router module.

flashcards.back: Re-fetches Server Components for the current route, keeping client state.

title: Dynamic Routes
description: Capture parts of the URL with [param], [...slug] and [[...slug]].

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Wrap a folder name in square brackets to create a dynamic segment. The value is passed to the page as `params`.

sections.title: Variants
sections.content:
- `[id]` — one segment: `/posts/42`.
- `[...slug]` — one or more segments: `/docs/a/b`.
- `[[...slug]]` — zero or more: also matches `/docs`.

sections.title: Async params
sections.content: Since Next.js 15, `params` and `searchParams` are Promises. Await them in Server Components, or use `use()` / `useParams()` in Client Components.

codeExamples.title: Reading params
codeExamples.explanation: The page awaits `params`, loads the post and calls `notFound()` (from next/navigation) when it doesn't exist.

commonMistakes: Accessing `params.slug` synchronously (deprecated in 15, removed in 16).
Forgetting to handle unknown ids with notFound().
realWorldExample: Product pages (`/products/[id]`) and docs sites (`/docs/[...slug]`) use dynamic routes.
interviewTip: Mention async params as a recent breaking change.

quiz.prompt: Which folder matches /docs, /docs/a and /docs/a/b?
quiz.explanation: Optional catch-all also matches the base path.

flashcards.front: Type of params in Next.js 15+ pages?

title: Route Groups
description: Organize routes and share layouts without affecting the URL.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: A folder wrapped in parentheses, like `(marketing)`, is a route group. It's left out of the URL path.

sections.title: Uses
sections.content:
- Organize routes by section or team.
- Give a subset of routes their own layout (e.g. `(auth)` pages without the main nav).
- Create **multiple root layouts** — each group has its own `layout.tsx` with `<html>` and `<body>`.

sections.title: Caveats
sections.content: Two groups must not resolve to the same URL. Navigating between different root layouts triggers a full page load.

codeExamples.title: Different layouts per section
codeExamples.code:
app/
  (marketing)/
    layout.tsx        # marketing header & footer
    page.tsx          # /
    pricing/page.tsx  # /pricing
  (app)/
    layout.tsx        # authenticated shell with sidebar
    dashboard/page.tsx  # /dashboard
codeExamples.explanation: Marketing pages and the app share no layout, yet URLs stay clean.

commonMistakes: Creating `(a)/about` and `(b)/about` — conflicting routes.
Expecting the group name to appear in the URL.
realWorldExample: SaaS products separate marketing, auth and app shells with route groups.
interviewTip: Mention multiple root layouts and the full reload caveat.

quiz.prompt: Route group names appear in the URL.
quiz.explanation: Parenthesized folders are omitted from the path.

title: Parallel Routes
description: Render multiple pages in the same layout at once with named slots.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Parallel routes let a layout render several pages simultaneously. Create slots with `@name` folders; each slot is passed to the parent layout as a prop.

sections.title: Why use them?
sections.content: Dashboards with independent panels, split views, and modals (combined with intercepting routes). Each slot can have its own `loading` and `error` states and navigate independently.

sections.title: default.js
sections.content: On a hard navigation (full page load), Next.js can't recover the active state of slots that don't match the URL, so it renders the slot's `default.js`. In Next.js 16 every slot must have an explicit `default.js` (return `null` or `notFound()`), otherwise the build fails.

codeExamples.title: Dashboard with two slots
codeExamples.explanation: `@analytics` and `@team` render side by side. Slots aren't URL segments, so `/dashboard` renders both.

commonMistakes: Forgetting `default.tsx`, causing 404s on refresh (and build errors in Next 16).
Thinking slots change the URL.
realWorldExample: Admin dashboards render metrics and activity panels as independent slots with separate loading skeletons.
interviewTip: Pair parallel routes with intercepting routes to explain the 'modal with shareable URL' pattern.

quiz.prompt: How is a parallel route slot defined?
quiz.explanation: Slots use the @ prefix.

flashcards.front: What does default.js do for a slot?
flashcards.back: Provides fallback UI when the slot's state can't be recovered from the URL.

title: Intercepting Routes
description: Load a route inside the current layout — e.g. open a photo in a modal while keeping a shareable URL.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Intercepting routes show a different route's content in the current context during **soft navigation** (clicking a Link). On a hard navigation (refresh, shared URL), the original full page renders.

sections.title: Conventions
sections.content:
Based on route segments (not file paths):

- `(.)` — same level
- `(..)` — one level up
- `(..)(..)` — two levels up
- `(...)` — from the app root

sections.title: The modal pattern
sections.content: Feed at `/feed`, photo page at `/photo/[id]`. Inside a `@modal` slot, `(..)photo/[id]` intercepts the navigation and shows the photo in a modal over the feed. Refreshing `/photo/123` shows the full photo page.

codeExamples.title: Folder structure for a modal
codeExamples.code:
app/
  layout.tsx            # renders {children} and {modal}
  feed/page.tsx
  photo/[id]/page.tsx   # full page (hard navigation)
  @modal/
    default.tsx         # returns null
    (.)photo/[id]/page.tsx  # modal (soft navigation)
codeExamples.explanation: Clicking a photo link in the feed renders the intercepted route in the modal slot; the URL updates to `/photo/123` so it's shareable.

commonMistakes: Using file-system levels instead of route segments to count (..).
Not closing the modal with router.back().
realWorldExample: Instagram-style photo modals and login modals use intercepting routes.
interviewTip: Explain soft vs hard navigation behaviour clearly.

quiz.prompt: When you refresh an intercepted URL, the modal version renders.
quiz.explanation: Hard navigation renders the original route's full page.

flashcards.front: Convention to intercept from the root?

title: not-found and notFound()
description: Render 404 UI for unknown routes and missing resources.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `not-found.tsx` defines the UI shown when `notFound()` is called in a segment, and the root `app/not-found.tsx` handles all unmatched URLs.

sections.title: When to call notFound()
sections.content: When a dynamic segment doesn't match data: a deleted product, an unknown slug. It throws, stops rendering and returns a 404 status (for non-streamed responses).

codeExamples.title: Missing product
codeExamples.explanation: Unknown ids render the segment's not-found UI with a 404 status, which is better for SEO than an empty page.

commonMistakes: Rendering 'Not found' text with a 200 status instead of calling notFound().
Wrapping notFound() in try/catch.
realWorldExample: E-commerce sites show friendly 404s with search suggestions for discontinued products.
interviewTip: Mention correct status codes matter for SEO.

quiz.prompt: notFound() throws to stop rendering the current segment.
quiz.explanation: Like redirect, it uses a special thrown error.

title: Layouts
description: Shared UI that wraps pages and persists across navigation.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: A layout is UI shared between multiple pages. It receives `children` (the page or nested layout) and stays mounted when navigating between its child routes.

sections.title: Root layout
sections.content: `app/layout.tsx` is required and must render `<html>` and `<body>`. Put global providers, fonts and metadata defaults here.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content:
- Layouts don't re-render on navigation, so they can't read the current pathname on the server (use a Client Component with `usePathname`).
- Layouts don't receive `searchParams`.
- Data fetching in layouts runs once per layout render; fetch where data is needed.

codeExamples.title: Root layout
codeExamples.explanation: The root layout sets the font, global CSS and a metadata title template that child pages fill in.

commonMistakes: Trying to read searchParams in a layout.
Making the root layout a Client Component.
realWorldExample: App shells with sidebars and top bars live in layouts so they don't flicker between pages.
interviewTip: Explain persistence and what layouts cannot access.

quiz.prompt: Which must the root layout render?
quiz.explanation: The root layout defines the document structure.

title: Nested Layouts
description: Layouts nest automatically along the route hierarchy.

sections.title: How it works
sections.content: A `layout.tsx` in any folder wraps all routes below it, and is itself wrapped by parent layouts. `/dashboard/settings` renders root layout → dashboard layout → settings page.

sections.title: Partial rendering
sections.content: When navigating between sibling routes, only the segments that change re-render. Shared layouts keep their state and aren't re-fetched.

codeExamples.title: Settings sub-layout with tabs
codeExamples.explanation: Switching between profile and billing keeps the tab nav and the outer dashboard layout mounted.

commonMistakes: Duplicating navigation in every page instead of using a nested layout.
realWorldExample: Settings pages with tabbed sub-navigation use nested layouts.
interviewTip: Mention partial rendering as a performance benefit.

quiz.prompt: Navigating between /dashboard/a and /dashboard/b re-renders the dashboard layout.
quiz.explanation: Shared layouts are preserved.

title: Templates
description: Like layouts, but re-mounted on every navigation.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `template.tsx` wraps children like a layout, but gets a unique key per route, so it **remounts** on navigation: state resets and Effects re-run.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.content:
- Enter/exit animations per page.
- Per-page analytics in useEffect.
- Resetting a form or feedback widget on each page.

Prefer layouts unless you specifically need the remount.

codeExamples.title: Fade-in per page
codeExamples.explanation: Because the template remounts on every navigation, the fade-in runs each time.

commonMistakes: Using templates by default, losing layout persistence benefits.
realWorldExample: Blogs use templates for page-transition animations.
interviewTip: Contrast layout (persist) vs template (remount).

quiz.prompt: What's the key difference between layout and template?
quiz.explanation: Templates get a new instance per navigation.

flashcards.back: Template state resets each navigation; layout state persists.

title: Loading UI
description: Instant loading states with loading.tsx and Suspense.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `loading.tsx` automatically wraps the segment's page in a `<Suspense>` boundary. Its UI shows immediately on navigation while the page's data loads, then streams in.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.content: Users get instant feedback; the layout stays interactive. For dynamic routes, the loading UI is prefetched so it appears without a network round-trip.

sections.title: Going further
sections.content: Use `<Suspense>` inside pages for finer control so fast sections show before slow ones.

codeExamples.title: Skeleton loader
codeExamples.explanation: Shown instantly while `app/dashboard/page.tsx` fetches. `aria-busy` informs assistive technologies.

commonMistakes: Only relying on one loading.tsx for a page with very different data speeds.
realWorldExample: Dashboards show skeleton cards while analytics queries run.
interviewTip: Explain that loading.tsx = automatic Suspense boundary + streaming.

quiz.prompt: loading.tsx wraps the page in a Suspense boundary.
quiz.explanation: It's a convention for a Suspense fallback.

flashcards.back: The Suspense fallback for its segment.

title: Error Handling UI
description: Catch errors per segment with error.tsx and global-error.tsx.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `error.tsx` creates a React error boundary around a segment's page (and nested children). It must be a Client Component and receives `error` and `reset`.

sections.title: Scope
sections.content: An `error.tsx` does not catch errors in the `layout` of the same segment — put it one level up for that. `global-error.tsx` catches errors in the root layout and must render its own `<html>` and `<body>`.

sections.title: Expected errors
sections.content: Model expected failures (validation, 'not found') as return values or `notFound()`, not thrown exceptions. Use error boundaries for unexpected errors.

codeExamples.title: Segment error boundary
codeExamples.explanation: `reset()` re-renders the segment. In production, server error messages are replaced with a generic message and a `digest` you can match in server logs.

commonMistakes: Forgetting 'use client' in error.tsx.
Expecting error.tsx to catch errors from the layout in the same folder.
realWorldExample: A failing analytics panel shows a retry button instead of crashing the whole dashboard.
interviewTip: Explain digest and why production hides server error messages (to avoid leaking secrets).

quiz.prompt: error.tsx can be a Server Component.
quiz.explanation: Error boundaries must be Client Components.

flashcards.front: Which file catches root layout errors?

title: Server Components in Next.js
description: In the App Router every component is a Server Component unless marked otherwise.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Pages, layouts and components in `app/` are React Server Components by default. They render on the server (at build time or per request) and send an RSC payload plus HTML to the browser.

sections.title: Benefits
sections.content:
- Fetch data directly with `await` — databases, CMS, internal services.
- Keep API keys and heavy libraries off the client.
- Less JavaScript to download and hydrate.
- Results can be cached and reused across requests.

sections.title: When you need a Client Component instead
sections.content: State, Effects, event handlers, browser APIs (`window`, `localStorage`), or client-only libraries.

codeExamples.title: Fetching on the server
codeExamples.explanation: No `useEffect`, no loading spinner state, no API route — the page awaits data and renders HTML on the server.

commonMistakes: Adding 'use client' just to fetch data.
Importing server-only modules (db clients) into Client Components.
realWorldExample: Blogs, docs and product listings are mostly Server Components with small client islands.
interviewTip: Mention that Server Components are the default and why that reduces bundle size.

quiz.prompt: In the App Router, components are Client Components unless marked with 'use server'.
quiz.explanation: They're Server Components by default; 'use client' marks client boundaries.

flashcards.front: What directive opts into a client boundary?

title: Keeping Code Server-Only
description: Prevent secrets and server code from leaking into client bundles.

sections.title: The risk
sections.content: A module that reads `process.env.DATABASE_URL` could accidentally be imported into a Client Component. Non-`NEXT_PUBLIC_` env vars become empty strings on the client, but the code itself still ships.

sections.title: The fix
sections.content: Add `import 'server-only'` at the top of server modules. If a Client Component imports them, the build fails with a clear error. The `client-only` package does the reverse.

sections.title: Data Access Layer
sections.content: Put all data access in a dedicated server-only layer that checks auth and returns **DTOs** (only the fields the UI needs), never raw database rows.

codeExamples.title: A server-only data module
codeExamples.explanation: The `server-only` import guards against client imports, and the function returns only safe fields.

commonMistakes: Passing full database objects to Client Components.
Prefixing secrets with NEXT_PUBLIC_.
realWorldExample: Teams keep `lib/data/*` server-only and review any new NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables in code review.
interviewTip: Mention 'server-only' and the DTO pattern; it shows security awareness.

quiz.prompt: What happens if a Client Component imports a module with `import 'server-only'`?
options: The build fails with an error
quiz.explanation: server-only causes a build-time error for client imports.

flashcards.back: A minimal object with only fields safe for the UI.

title: Server & Client Composition Patterns
description: Interleave Server and Client Components effectively.

sections.title: Pattern 1: push client components to the leaves
sections.content: Keep layouts and pages on the server; make only the interactive bits (search box, like button) client components.

sections.title: Pattern 2: pass Server Components as children
sections.content: A Client Component can't import a Server Component, but it can receive one as `children`. The server renders it and React slots it into the client tree.

sections.title: Pattern 3: providers
sections.content: Context only works in Client Components. Create a `'use client'` `Providers` component and render it in the root layout around `{children}` — children stay Server Components.

sections.title: Pattern 4: share data with React cache()
sections.content: Need the same data in a layout and a page? Call a function wrapped in React's `cache()`; duplicate calls in one request are deduplicated.

codeExamples.title: Client wrapper with server children
codeExamples.explanation: `ServerRenderedStats` still runs on the server; `Collapsible` only controls whether its already-rendered output is shown.

commonMistakes: Wrapping the whole app in 'use client' to use one context.
Passing functions from Server to Client Components (not serializable).
realWorldExample: Theme and auth providers wrap `{children}` in the root layout while pages remain server-rendered.
interviewTip: The children pattern is a favourite interview question — be ready to explain why it works.

quiz.prompt: A Client Component can render a Server Component passed to it as children.
quiz.explanation: The server renders it; the client receives the result.

flashcards.front: How to use Context with Server Components?
flashcards.back: Wrap children in a 'use client' provider component.

title: Client Components in Next.js
description: Interactive components that are pre-rendered on the server and hydrated in the browser.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: A file starting with `'use client'` (and everything it imports) becomes part of the client bundle. These components render to HTML on the server for the first load, then hydrate.

sections.title: When to use
sections.content:
- State and lifecycle: `useState`, `useEffect`, `useReducer`.
- Event listeners: `onClick`, `onChange`.
- Browser-only APIs: geolocation, localStorage, IntersectionObserver.
- Client-only libraries (charts, maps, animation).

sections.title: Browser APIs safely
sections.content: Because Client Components also render on the server, access `window` inside `useEffect` or event handlers. For libraries that crash on the server, use `next/dynamic` with `ssr: false` (inside a Client Component).

codeExamples.title: Loading a client-only map
codeExamples.explanation: The map library only loads in the browser, avoiding `window is not defined` errors during server rendering.

commonMistakes: Accessing window during render.
Using `ssr: false` in a Server Component (not allowed).
realWorldExample: Store locators, rich editors and charts are typical client components.
interviewTip: Clarify 'Client Components still SSR' — a common misconception.

quiz.prompt: Client Components are rendered to HTML on the server during the initial page load.
quiz.explanation: They pre-render then hydrate.

flashcards.front: Load a client-only library without SSR?
flashcards.back: next/dynamic with ssr: false inside a Client Component.

title: The 'use client' Boundary
description: Understand exactly what the directive does and where to put it.

sections.title: What it does
sections.content: `'use client'` declares a boundary in the **module graph**. The file and all modules it imports are bundled for the client. It doesn't need to be in every client file — only in files imported by server code.

sections.title: Props across the boundary
sections.content: Props from Server to Client Components must be serializable: strings, numbers, plain objects, arrays, Dates, Maps, Sets, JSX, Promises, and Server Functions. Not regular functions or class instances.

sections.title: Third-party components
sections.content: Some libraries use hooks but lack the directive. Re-export them from your own file with `'use client'` so they can be used in Server Components.

codeExamples.title: Wrapping a third-party component
codeExamples.explanation: The wrapper marks the boundary so the hook-based library runs on the client.

commonMistakes: Sprinkling 'use client' in every file 'just in case'.
Passing an onClick function from a Server Component to a Client Component.
realWorldExample: Design system libraries ship with 'use client' on interactive components so they work in RSC apps.
interviewTip: Explain module-graph boundaries rather than per-component flags.

quiz.prompt: Which prop can a Server Component pass to a Client Component?
quiz.explanation: Plain serializable objects can cross the boundary.

flashcards.back: At the very top of the file, before imports.

title: Data Fetching in the App Router
description: Fetch on the server with async components, in parallel, close to where data is used.

sections.title: Server-first fetching
sections.content: Make Server Components `async` and `await` data. Use `fetch`, an ORM, or any SDK. `fetch` calls with the same URL and options in one render are memoized automatically; wrap ORM calls in React's `cache()` for the same deduplication.

sections.title: Avoid waterfalls
sections.content: Sequential awaits wait for each other. Start independent requests together with `Promise.all`, or split into separate components with their own Suspense boundaries so each streams independently.

sections.title: Fetching on the client
sections.content: For data that changes with user interaction (infinite scroll, live search), use a client library like SWR or TanStack Query, or pass a promise from the server and read it with `use()`.

codeExamples.title: Parallel requests
codeExamples.explanation: Both requests run simultaneously, so the page waits for the slowest one rather than the sum of both.

commonMistakes: Fetching your own Route Handlers from Server Components (an unnecessary network hop) — call the data function directly.
Sequential awaits for independent data.
realWorldExample: A product page fetches product, reviews and recommendations in parallel; reviews stream later inside Suspense.
interviewTip: Name request memoization, Promise.all, and Suspense streaming as tools against waterfalls.

quiz.prompt: A Server Component should fetch from your own /api route handler to get data.
quiz.explanation: Call the data source directly; the extra HTTP hop is unnecessary.

flashcards.front: Dedupe ORM calls within a request with…

beforeAfter.title: Fix the waterfall
beforeAfter.explanation: The 'before' version takes the sum of all three latencies; the 'after' version takes only the slowest.

title: Integrating External APIs
description: Call third-party and internal APIs safely from the server.

sections.title: Where to call APIs
sections.content: Call APIs from Server Components, Server Actions or Route Handlers so keys stay secret and responses can be cached. Only call from the client when the API is public and user-specific interaction demands it.

sections.title: Robust calls
sections.content:
- Check `res.ok` and throw or handle non-2xx responses.
- Add timeouts with `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`.
- Validate the response shape (e.g. Zod) instead of trusting it.
- Decide caching explicitly: `cache: 'force-cache'`, `next: { revalidate: 3600 }`, or `"use cache"` with Cache Components.

codeExamples.title: A typed, cached API helper
codeExamples.explanation: The key stays on the server, the response is cached for 10 minutes, slow requests abort after 5 seconds, and the data is validated.

commonMistakes: Exposing API keys via NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables.
Ignoring non-2xx responses.
realWorldExample: Dashboards aggregate Stripe, GitHub and analytics APIs on the server and cache results.
interviewTip: Mention secrets, validation, timeouts and caching strategy.

quiz.prompt: Best place to call an API that needs a secret key?
options: Inline in JSX on the client
A Server Component or Server Action
quiz.explanation: Server code keeps the key private.

title: Database Integration
description: Query databases directly from server code with an ORM or query builder.

sections.title: The basics
sections.content: Server Components and Server Actions can import a database client directly. Popular choices: Prisma, Drizzle, Kysely, or provider SDKs (Neon, Supabase, PlanetScale).

sections.title: Connections
sections.content: In development, hot reloading can create many clients — store a single instance on `globalThis`. In serverless environments, use pooled or HTTP-based drivers to avoid exhausting connections.

sections.title: Organize access
sections.content: Put queries in a server-only Data Access Layer that checks authorization, returns DTOs and is wrapped in `cache()` where useful.

codeExamples.title: Singleton client + query
codeExamples.explanation: One client per process avoids connection storms during development. The page maps rows to minimal objects before passing them to a component.

commonMistakes: Creating a new database client on every request.
Querying the database from Client Components (impossible — and a sign of mixed boundaries).
realWorldExample: SaaS apps use Drizzle or Prisma with serverless Postgres from Server Components and Actions.
interviewTip: Mention connection pooling in serverless and the DAL pattern.

quiz.prompt: You can import a database client directly into a Server Component.
quiz.explanation: Server Components run only on the server.

flashcards.front: Why store the client on globalThis in dev?
flashcards.back: To avoid creating new connections on every hot reload.

title: Caching Overview
description: How Next.js caches data and rendered output — and how Next.js 16's Cache Components change it.

sections.title: Why caching matters
sections.content: Caching avoids repeating work — fetching, rendering — for every request, making pages faster and cheaper. The challenge is keeping cached data fresh.

sections.title: The layers
sections.content:
- **Request memoization:** identical `fetch` calls (and `cache()`-wrapped functions) in one render run once.
- **Data cache:** persisted results of cached fetches/functions across requests and deployments.
- **Full route cache:** pre-rendered HTML and RSC payload for static routes.
- **Client router cache:** RSC payloads kept in the browser during a session for instant back/forward.

sections.title: Defaults changed
sections.content: Since Next.js 15, `fetch` requests and GET Route Handlers are **not cached by default**. You opt in with `cache: 'force-cache'`, `next: { revalidate }`, or route segment config.

sections.title: Cache Components (Next.js 16)
sections.content: With `cacheComponents: true` in `next.config`, rendering is dynamic by default and you opt into caching with the `"use cache"` directive on files, components or functions, tuned with `cacheLife()` and tagged with `cacheTag()`. Static parts are prerendered into a shell, and dynamic parts stream in through Suspense (this replaces the experimental PPR flag).

codeExamples.title: Opting into caching (classic model)
codeExamples.explanation: Each fetch states its freshness. The tag lets a Server Action invalidate posts on demand with `revalidateTag('posts', 'max')`.

commonMistakes: Assuming fetch is cached by default (true in Next 14, not in 15+).
Caching user-specific data in a shared cache.
realWorldExample: Content sites cache CMS data for hours and revalidate instantly via a CMS webhook calling revalidateTag.
interviewTip: Name the layers, mention the Next 15 default change, and show awareness of 'use cache' in Next 16.

quiz.prompt: In Next.js 15+, fetch requests are cached by default.
quiz.explanation: They default to no caching; opt in explicitly.

quiz.prompt: Which directive enables caching with Cache Components in Next.js 16?
quiz.explanation: "use cache" marks cacheable functions, components or files.

flashcards.back: Request memoization, data cache, full route cache, client router cache.

title: Revalidation
description: Keep cached data fresh with time-based and on-demand revalidation.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Revalidation refreshes cached data and pages. It's how static pages stay up to date without rebuilding the whole site (historically called ISR — Incremental Static Regeneration).

sections.title: Time-based
sections.content: `fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 60 } })`, `export const revalidate = 60` in a segment, or `cacheLife()` with `"use cache"`. After the time passes, the next request still gets the stale version while a fresh one is generated in the background (stale-while-revalidate).

sections.title: On-demand
sections.content:
- `revalidatePath('/blog')` — invalidate a route.
- `revalidateTag('posts', 'max')` — invalidate data tagged `posts` with stale-while-revalidate semantics (Next 16 requires a cache-life profile as the second argument).
- `updateTag('posts')` (Next 16, Server Actions only) — expire immediately so the user sees their own write.

codeExamples.title: Revalidate after a mutation
codeExamples.explanation: `updateTag` gives read-your-own-writes semantics in a Server Action. A CMS webhook in a Route Handler would use `revalidateTag('posts', 'max')` instead.

commonMistakes: Using very short revalidate times on everything, defeating caching.
Forgetting to revalidate after mutations, showing stale data.
realWorldExample: News sites revalidate article pages when editors hit publish via a webhook.
interviewTip: Explain stale-while-revalidate and time-based vs on-demand.

quiz.prompt: After a revalidate period expires, what does the next visitor get?
options: Always a freshly built page with a delay
The stale page while a fresh one regenerates in the background
quiz.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate serves cached content and regenerates in the background.

interviewQuestion.question: What is revalidation in Next.js?
interviewQuestion.answer: It's refreshing cached data or pre-rendered pages. Time-based revalidation regenerates content in the background after a period; on-demand revalidation (revalidatePath, revalidateTag, updateTag) invalidates it immediately after an event such as a CMS publish or a mutation.

title: 'use cache' & Cache Components
description: Next.js 16's explicit caching model: dynamic by default, cache what you choose.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Cache Components is an opt-in mode (`cacheComponents: true`) where every route is dynamic unless you mark code with `"use cache"`. Cached output can be part of the prerendered static shell; uncached, request-specific parts stream in through `<Suspense>`.

sections.title: How to use it
sections.content:
- Add `"use cache"` at the top of a file, an async component, or an async function.
- Arguments and closed-over values become part of the cache key.
- Set lifetimes with `cacheLife('minutes' | 'hours' | 'days' | ...)` or custom profiles.
- Tag entries with `cacheTag('product-42')` for on-demand invalidation.

sections.title: Rules
sections.content: Don't read request-specific APIs (`cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`) inside a cached scope — read them outside and pass values in. Uncached dynamic access must be wrapped in Suspense so the static shell can still be produced.

codeExamples.title: Caching a product component
codeExamples.explanation: Product details are cached for hours and tagged for invalidation. The cart reads cookies, so it stays dynamic and streams inside Suspense.

commonMistakes: Reading cookies() inside a 'use cache' function.
Assuming route segment config like `export const dynamic` still applies with Cache Components (it's replaced).
realWorldExample: E-commerce pages cache product data but keep the cart and personalized recommendations dynamic.
interviewTip: Explain the mental model flip: in Next 16 with Cache Components, dynamic is the default and caching is explicit.

quiz.prompt: You can call cookies() inside a function marked 'use cache'.
quiz.explanation: Request-specific data must be read outside the cached scope and passed in.

flashcards.front: What becomes part of a 'use cache' key?
flashcards.back: Its arguments and any closed-over values (plus build id).

title: Static Rendering
description: Render routes at build time (or during revalidation) and serve them from cache/CDN.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: With static rendering, a route's HTML and RSC payload are generated at build time or in the background after revalidation, then served to every user from cache.

sections.title: When is a route static?
sections.content: When it doesn't use request-time information: no `cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`, uncached fetches, or `connection()`. Next.js decides automatically per route.

sections.title: Benefits
sections.content: Fastest possible responses (served from the edge), cheap to run, resilient under traffic spikes.

codeExamples.title: A static marketing page
codeExamples.explanation: The fetch is cached and nothing request-specific is read, so the page is rendered at build time.

commonMistakes: Accidentally making a static page dynamic by reading searchParams in a deeply nested component.
Statically rendering user-specific content.
realWorldExample: Marketing pages, docs and blogs are statically rendered and served from CDNs.
interviewTip: Explain what opts a route out of static rendering.

quiz.prompt: Which makes a route dynamic?
quiz.explanation: cookies() depends on the incoming request.

flashcards.front: Where are static pages typically served from?

interviewQuestion.question: What is static rendering?
interviewQuestion.answer: Generating a route's output ahead of time (at build or revalidation) and serving the same cached result to all users. It's the fastest option and works for any content that isn't personalized per request.

title: Dynamic Rendering
description: Render per request when output depends on the user or the request.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Dynamic rendering produces the route on each request. It's needed when output depends on who is asking or on per-request data.

sections.title: What triggers it
sections.content:
- Dynamic APIs: `cookies()`, `headers()`, `draftMode()`, `searchParams`, `connection()`.
- Uncached data (`cache: 'no-store'`, or simply not cached in Next 15+).
- `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` (classic model).

sections.title: Mixing static and dynamic
sections.content: You don't have to choose for the whole page: with Suspense (and Cache Components in Next 16) the static shell is served instantly and dynamic parts stream in.

codeExamples.title: Personalized greeting
codeExamples.explanation: Reading cookies makes this route dynamic: it renders on every request with the visitor's own name.

commonMistakes: Making a whole page dynamic for one small personalized widget — isolate it in Suspense.
Forgetting to await cookies() (async since Next 15).
realWorldExample: Dashboards, carts and account pages render dynamically.
interviewTip: Compare static vs dynamic with examples and mention streaming as the middle ground.

quiz.prompt: cookies() must be awaited in Next.js 15+.
quiz.explanation: Dynamic APIs are async.

flashcards.front: API to explicitly opt into dynamic rendering without reading data?

interviewQuestion.question: What is dynamic rendering?
interviewQuestion.answer: Rendering a route at request time because it depends on request data such as cookies, headers or search params, or on uncached data. It enables personalization at the cost of per-request work.

title: Streaming in Next.js
description: Progressively send UI from the server with loading.tsx and Suspense.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Streaming breaks a page into chunks. The server sends the shell and ready content first, then streams each Suspense boundary's content as its data resolves.

sections.title: How to use it
sections.content:
- Route level: add `loading.tsx`.
- Component level: wrap slow components in `<Suspense fallback>`.
- Make slow components fetch their own data so they don't block siblings.

sections.title: SEO and status codes
sections.content: Streamed content is still in the HTML response that crawlers receive. Once streaming starts, the status code is already 200, so redirects/notFound inside streamed parts are handled with client-side instructions.

codeExamples.title: Independent streaming sections
codeExamples.explanation: The revenue card appears after ~200ms; invoices stream in later without blocking it.

commonMistakes: Fetching all data in the page component, which blocks every boundary.
Too many tiny boundaries causing layout shift.
realWorldExample: Analytics dashboards stream fast KPIs first and slow tables later.
interviewTip: Connect streaming with Suspense and component-level data fetching.

quiz.prompt: Streamed content is invisible to search engine crawlers.
quiz.explanation: It's part of the HTML response.

flashcards.front: Two ways to stream in Next.js?

title: generateStaticParams
description: Pre-render dynamic routes at build time.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `generateStaticParams` returns a list of params for a dynamic segment. Next.js statically generates those paths at build time. It's the App Router replacement for `getStaticPaths`.

sections.title: Unlisted params
sections.content: By default, params not returned are rendered on demand at request time and then cached. Set `export const dynamicParams = false` to return 404 for them instead.

sections.title: Strategy
sections.content: For large sites, pre-render the most popular pages and let the rest render on demand. Return an empty array to render all on first visit.

codeExamples.title: Pre-render blog posts
codeExamples.explanation: Every post returned is built ahead of time; new posts published later render on first request.

commonMistakes: Generating hundreds of thousands of pages at build time, causing very slow builds.
Returning params with the wrong key names.
realWorldExample: Docs sites generate every page at build; e-commerce pre-renders top products.
interviewTip: Mention it replaces getStaticPaths and explain dynamicParams.

quiz.prompt: What does `export const dynamicParams = false` do?
options: Returns 404 for params not returned by generateStaticParams
quiz.explanation: Only pre-generated params are allowed.

title: Server Actions in Next.js
description: Mutate data from forms and buttons with server functions — no API route needed.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Server Actions are async functions marked with `'use server'` that run on the server. Pass them to `<form action>` or call them from Client Components (usually inside `startTransition`).

sections.title: Why use them?
sections.content:
- No hand-written API route or fetch call for mutations.
- Forms work before JavaScript loads (progressive enhancement).
- After a mutation you can revalidate or redirect, and Next.js returns the updated UI in the same round-trip.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: Each action is a public POST endpoint. Validate input, check authentication and authorization inside the action. Next.js adds protections (encrypted action ids, origin checks, dead-code elimination of unused actions), but authorization is your job.

codeExamples.title: Add a comment
codeExamples.explanation: `bind` pre-fills the post id (bound arguments are encrypted). The action verifies the session, validates, writes and revalidates the page.

commonMistakes: Skipping authorization because the form is only shown to admins.
Using Server Actions for data fetching — they're designed for mutations and run sequentially.
realWorldExample: Todo apps, comment boxes, settings forms and 'like' buttons use Server Actions.
interviewTip: Highlight both DX (no API boilerplate) and the security model.

quiz.prompt: Server Actions are good for fetching data in Client Components.
quiz.explanation: They're intended for mutations; fetch data in Server Components.

flashcards.front: How to pass extra args to a form action?

interviewQuestion.question: What are Server Actions?
interviewQuestion.answer: Async server functions marked with 'use server' that the client can invoke, typically from forms. They handle mutations, can revalidate caches and redirect, and work without client JavaScript when used as a form action. They must validate input and check auth because they are callable endpoints.

title: Forms, Validation & Pending States
description: Build robust forms with Server Actions, useActionState and useFormStatus.

sections.title: The pattern
sections.content:
1. Server Action validates with a schema and returns `{ errors }` or `{ success }`.
2. Client form uses `useActionState(action, initialState)` to display errors and pending state.
3. A submit button uses `useFormStatus()` (or `isPending`) to disable itself.
4. Optionally `useOptimistic` for instant feedback.

sections.title: Why return errors instead of throwing?
sections.content: Validation failures are expected. Returning them keeps the form state, while thrown errors hit the error boundary.

codeExamples.title: Validated sign-up form
codeExamples.explanation: The server validates and returns field errors; the client shows them and disables the button while pending.

commonMistakes: Only validating on the client.
Throwing for validation errors and losing form input.
realWorldExample: Checkout and onboarding forms in Next.js apps commonly use this exact pattern.
interviewTip: Show how server validation, useActionState and pending UI fit together.

quiz.prompt: Where should validation that protects your database happen?
options: On the server inside the action
quiz.explanation: Client validation is UX; server validation is security.

title: Route Handlers
description: Build HTTP endpoints with route.ts using the Web Request/Response APIs.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: A `route.ts` file exports functions named after HTTP methods. It's the App Router's equivalent of API routes and uses standard `Request` and `Response` objects.

sections.title: When to use them
sections.content:
- Webhooks (Stripe, CMS) and public APIs for other clients (mobile apps).
- Non-HTML responses: RSS, files, JSON for third parties.
- OAuth callbacks.

For your own UI's mutations, Server Actions are usually simpler; for data reads, use Server Components directly.

sections.title: Caching
sections.content: Since Next.js 15, GET handlers are dynamic by default. Opt into static with `export const dynamic = 'force-static'` (classic model) or `"use cache"` helpers with Cache Components.

codeExamples.title: A webhook handler
codeExamples.explanation: The handler authenticates the webhook, invalidates the matching cache tag and returns JSON.

commonMistakes: Placing route.ts and page.tsx in the same folder.
Calling your own route handlers from Server Components instead of calling the logic directly.
realWorldExample: Stripe payment webhooks and RSS feeds are implemented as Route Handlers.
interviewTip: Explain when to choose Route Handlers vs Server Actions.

quiz.prompt: Which file defines an API endpoint in the App Router?
quiz.explanation: route.ts exports HTTP method handlers.

flashcards.front: Are GET route handlers cached by default in Next 15+?

title: Proxy (formerly Middleware)
description: Run code before a request is completed: redirects, rewrites, headers — renamed to proxy.ts in Next.js 16.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Code that runs before routes render, for every matching request. In Next.js 16 the convention was renamed from `middleware.ts` to **`proxy.ts`** (export a `proxy` function) to clarify its role at the network boundary. `middleware.ts` still works but is deprecated; proxy runs on the Node.js runtime.

sections.title: Good uses
sections.content:
- Redirects and rewrites (A/B tests, locale routing, legacy URLs).
- Setting headers and cookies.
- Optimistic auth checks: redirect if there's no session cookie at all.

sections.title: What not to do
sections.content: Don't rely on it as your only authorization layer or do slow database work there. A 2025 vulnerability (CVE-2025-29927) allowed middleware to be bypassed with a crafted header; authorize again where data is accessed.

codeExamples.title: Redirect unauthenticated users
codeExamples.explanation: Only matching paths run the proxy. It performs a cheap cookie check; real authorization still happens in the data layer.

commonMistakes: Doing heavy DB queries in proxy, adding latency to every request.
Treating proxy checks as sufficient authorization.
realWorldExample: International sites redirect `/` to `/en` or `/de` based on the Accept-Language header.
interviewTip: Mentioning the Next 16 rename and the 2025 bypass CVE shows up-to-date knowledge.

quiz.prompt: In Next.js 16, middleware.ts was renamed to proxy.ts.
quiz.explanation: middleware.ts is deprecated in favour of proxy.ts.

quiz.prompt: Which is the best use of proxy?
quiz.explanation: Keep it fast and lightweight.

flashcards.front: Config option to limit where proxy runs?

title: Cookies
description: Read and write cookies with the async cookies() API.

sections.title: Reading
sections.content: `const cookieStore = await cookies()` then `cookieStore.get('theme')?.value`. Reading cookies makes a route dynamic.

sections.title: Writing
sections.content: You can only **set** or **delete** cookies in Server Actions, Route Handlers or proxy — not while rendering a Server Component, because headers are already being streamed.

sections.title: Secure session cookies
sections.content: Use `httpOnly: true` (no JavaScript access), `secure: true` (HTTPS only), `sameSite: 'lax'` and an expiry.

codeExamples.title: Set a theme cookie in an action
codeExamples.explanation: The action sets a long-lived, secure cookie. The layout can read it with `await cookies()` to render the right theme on the server.

commonMistakes: Trying to set cookies inside a Server Component render.
Storing sensitive data in non-httpOnly cookies.
realWorldExample: Theme, locale and session tokens are commonly stored in cookies.
interviewTip: Mention async cookies() and where writes are allowed.

quiz.prompt: You can call cookieStore.set() while rendering a Server Component.
quiz.explanation: Set cookies in Server Actions, Route Handlers or proxy.

flashcards.front: Cookie flag that blocks JS access?

title: Headers
description: Read request headers and set response headers.

sections.title: Reading request headers
sections.content: `const h = await headers(); h.get('user-agent')`. The returned object is read-only, and using it makes the route dynamic.

sections.title: Setting response headers
sections.content:
- Route Handlers: `new Response(body, { headers: {...} })`.
- proxy: `NextResponse.next({ headers })` or `response.headers.set()`.
- Static headers for many routes: the `headers()` function in `next.config`.

sections.title: Security headers
sections.content: Set Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy for production apps.

codeExamples.title: Security headers in config
codeExamples.explanation: These headers apply to every route and harden the app against common attacks.

commonMistakes: Trying to mutate the object returned by headers().
Forgetting headers() is async.
realWorldExample: Apps read `x-forwarded-for` for rate limiting and set CSP headers for security audits.
interviewTip: Mention read-only request headers and where response headers are set.

quiz.prompt: Where do you configure static response headers for many routes?
quiz.explanation: next.config supports a headers() function.

title: Authentication
description: Verify who the user is: sign-in, sessions and libraries.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Authentication verifies identity — "who are you?" In Next.js it typically involves a sign-up/sign-in form, creating a session, and checking the session on each request.

sections.title: Session strategies
sections.content:
- **Stateless:** a signed/encrypted token (JWT/JWE) in an httpOnly cookie.
- **Database sessions:** a session id cookie that maps to a row in the database (easy revocation).

sections.title: Use a library
sections.content: Auth.js (NextAuth), Clerk, Better Auth, Supabase Auth, WorkOS and others handle OAuth, password hashing, CSRF and session rotation. Rolling your own is risky.

sections.title: Where to check
sections.content: Optimistic checks in proxy for redirects; secure checks in a `verifySession()` helper (wrapped in React `cache()`) called from the Data Access Layer, Server Actions and Route Handlers.

codeExamples.title: A cached session check
codeExamples.explanation: `cache()` deduplicates the check within a request, so layouts, pages and data functions can all call it cheaply.

commonMistakes: Checking auth only in a layout — layouts don't re-render on navigation and don't protect data fetched elsewhere.
Storing session tokens in localStorage.
realWorldExample: Most Next.js SaaS apps use Auth.js or Clerk with httpOnly session cookies.
interviewTip: Separate authentication (identity) from authorization (permissions), and mention checking close to data.

quiz.prompt: Checking the session only in the root layout is enough to protect all data.
quiz.explanation: Layouts don't re-run on every navigation and don't guard Server Actions or Route Handlers.

flashcards.back: To deduplicate the check within one request.

title: Authorization
description: Decide what an authenticated user may do — and enforce it on the server.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Authorization answers "what are you allowed to do?" — e.g. only admins can delete users, only the author can edit a post.

sections.title: Where to enforce
sections.content:
- In the Data Access Layer before returning data.
- In every Server Action and Route Handler before mutating.
- Hiding buttons in the UI improves UX but is never security.

sections.title: Ownership checks
sections.content: Don't trust ids from the client. Query with both the resource id **and** the current user's id (or verify ownership) to prevent IDOR (insecure direct object reference) bugs.

codeExamples.title: Ownership check in an action
codeExamples.explanation: The action verifies the session and checks ownership or admin role before deleting.

commonMistakes: Relying on hidden UI to protect admin actions.
Trusting a userId sent from the client.
realWorldExample: Multi-tenant SaaS apps scope every query by organization id from the session.
interviewTip: Mention IDOR and enforcing checks at the data layer.

quiz.prompt: A user can delete any post by changing the id in a request. What's the bug?
quiz.explanation: The server must verify the user owns the resource.

flashcards.front: Is hiding a button a security measure?
flashcards.back: No — enforce permissions on the server.

title: Environment Variables
description: Configure secrets and settings per environment.

sections.title: How they work
sections.content: Next.js loads `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.development`, `.env.production`. Variables are available on the server via `process.env`.

sections.title: Client exposure
sections.content: Only variables prefixed with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` are exposed to the browser, and they're **inlined at build time** — changing them requires a rebuild. Never put secrets in `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables.

sections.title: Best practices
sections.content:
- Keep `.env.local` out of git; commit an `.env.example`.
- Validate env vars at startup (e.g. with Zod or `@t3-oss/env-nextjs`).
- Set production values in your hosting dashboard.

codeExamples.title: Server vs public variables
codeExamples.code:
# .env.local
DATABASE_URL="postgres://..."          # server only
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY="sk_live_..."        # server only
NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID="G-12345"     # inlined into client JS
codeExamples.explanation: Only `NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID` reaches the browser. The others are undefined in client code.

commonMistakes: Prefixing secrets with NEXT_PUBLIC_.
Expecting NEXT_PUBLIC_ values to change at runtime without rebuilding.
realWorldExample: Teams store Stripe secret keys server-side and only expose publishable keys with NEXT_PUBLIC_.
interviewTip: Mention build-time inlining — a frequent gotcha.

quiz.prompt: Changing a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable on the server takes effect without a rebuild.
quiz.explanation: Public vars are inlined into the bundle at build time.

flashcards.front: Prefix that exposes a variable to the browser?

title: Metadata API
description: Define titles, descriptions and social cards with the metadata export.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Export a `metadata` object from a layout or page to set `<head>` tags. Next.js merges metadata from layouts down to pages.

sections.title: Features
sections.content:
- Title templates: `title: { template: '%s | Acme', default: 'Acme' }`.
- Open Graph and Twitter cards for link previews.
- `metadataBase` to resolve relative URLs.
- File conventions: `favicon.ico`, `opengraph-image.png` (or `.tsx` to generate), `robots.ts`, `sitemap.ts`.

sections.title: Rules
sections.content: Metadata exports are only supported in Server Components.

codeExamples.title: Static metadata
codeExamples.explanation: With the root layout's template, the page title becomes "About | Acme".

commonMistakes: Exporting metadata from a Client Component.
Using the same title on every page.
realWorldExample: Every marketing page sets unique titles, descriptions and OG images for search and social sharing.
interviewTip: Mention merging, templates and file-based metadata.

quiz.prompt: You can export metadata from a 'use client' page.
quiz.explanation: Metadata exports require Server Components.

flashcards.front: What does a title template do?

title: generateMetadata
description: Create metadata from dynamic data such as a product or post.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `export async function generateMetadata({ params, searchParams }, parent)` returns metadata computed from data. Use it when titles depend on route params.

sections.title: Performance
sections.content: Data requests used by both `generateMetadata` and the page are memoized (fetch, or functions wrapped in `cache()`), so you don't pay twice. Next.js can stream metadata for regular browsers while ensuring bots receive it in the head.

codeExamples.title: Product metadata
codeExamples.explanation: `cache()` ensures one database query serves both metadata and page.

commonMistakes: Fetching the same data twice without memoization.
Using both a metadata object and generateMetadata in the same file (not allowed).
realWorldExample: Blog posts and product pages generate unique titles and share images per item.
interviewTip: Mention deduplication via cache()/fetch memoization.

quiz.prompt: Can a file export both `metadata` and `generateMetadata`?
quiz.explanation: Choose one per segment.

flashcards.front: How to avoid duplicate queries in generateMetadata + page?
flashcards.back: Wrap the data function in React cache().

title: SEO in Next.js
description: Rendering, metadata, sitemaps and performance — everything search engines care about.

sections.title: Foundations
sections.content:
- Pre-rendered HTML (static or dynamic) so crawlers see content.
- Unique titles and descriptions; canonical URLs (`alternates.canonical`).
- Semantic headings and descriptive links.
- Correct status codes (`notFound()`, `permanentRedirect()`).

sections.title: Discovery files
sections.content: `app/sitemap.ts` and `app/robots.ts` generate `sitemap.xml` and `robots.txt` from code.

sections.title: Rich results
sections.content: Add JSON-LD structured data with a `<script type="application/ld+json">` in your page.

sections.title: Performance is SEO
sections.content: Google uses Core Web Vitals as a ranking signal: optimize images, fonts and JavaScript.

codeExamples.title: Generated sitemap
codeExamples.explanation: The sitemap updates automatically as posts are added.

commonMistakes: Client-only rendering of important content.
Soft 404s: rendering 'not found' with a 200 status.
realWorldExample: E-commerce sites generate sitemaps with tens of thousands of product URLs and Product JSON-LD.
interviewTip: Cover rendering, metadata, sitemaps, structured data and performance.

quiz.prompt: Which file generates robots.txt in the App Router?
quiz.explanation: app/robots.ts returns robots rules.

title: Image Optimization with next/image
description: Automatically resize, lazy-load and serve modern image formats.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: The `` component from `next/image` extends `` with automatic optimization: responsive sizes, modern formats (WebP/AVIF), lazy loading, and layout-shift prevention.

sections.title: Key props
sections.content:
- `width` and `height` (or `fill` with a sized parent) to reserve space and avoid CLS.
- `sizes` to tell the browser how wide the image displays, so it picks the right file.
- `priority` (or `preload` in newer versions) for the LCP image above the fold.
- `placeholder="blur"` for a blurred preview.

sections.title: Remote images
sections.content: Allow external hosts with `images.remotePatterns` in `next.config` (the old `domains` option is deprecated).

codeExamples.title: Responsive hero image
codeExamples.explanation: The static import supplies dimensions and a blur placeholder; `priority` loads it eagerly because it's the LCP element.

commonMistakes: Missing alt text.
Lazy-loading the LCP hero image (no priority).
Forgetting `sizes` with `fill`, making the browser download huge images.
realWorldExample: E-commerce product grids cut image bytes dramatically by serving correctly sized AVIF/WebP.
interviewTip: Mention CLS prevention, sizes, and prioritizing the LCP image.

quiz.prompt: Which prop should you set on the above-the-fold hero image?
quiz.explanation: Prioritize the LCP image so it loads early.

flashcards.front: Config for allowed remote image hosts?

title: Font Optimization with next/font
description: Self-host fonts with zero layout shift and no extra network requests to Google.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `next/font` downloads font files at build time and serves them from your own domain. It applies `size-adjust` fallbacks to prevent layout shift, and the browser never contacts Google Fonts at runtime (good for privacy and speed).

sections.title: Usage
sections.content: Call the font function at module scope, then use `className` or a CSS `variable`. Variable fonts are recommended. Use `next/font/local` for custom font files.

codeExamples.title: Two fonts as CSS variables
codeExamples.explanation: CSS can use `var(--font-sans)` and `var(--font-mono)`. Fonts are self-hosted and preloaded.

commonMistakes: Calling the font loader inside a component (must be module scope).
Linking Google Fonts CSS manually alongside next/font.
realWorldExample: Marketing sites remove font-related layout shift by switching to next/font.
interviewTip: Mention self-hosting, privacy, and CLS prevention.

quiz.prompt: next/font makes the browser request fonts from fonts.googleapis.com at runtime.
quiz.explanation: Fonts are downloaded at build time and self-hosted.

title: Next.js Performance Checklist
description: Practical steps to make Next.js apps fast.

sections.title: Rendering
sections.content:
- Keep most UI in Server Components; push 'use client' to leaves.
- Cache what you can (static rendering, `"use cache"`, revalidation).
- Stream slow sections with Suspense instead of blocking the page.
- Avoid request waterfalls (parallel fetches).

sections.title: Assets
sections.content:
- `next/image` with correct `sizes`, prioritize LCP image.
- `next/font` for fonts.
- `next/script` with `strategy="lazyOnload"` or `afterInteractive` for third-party scripts.

sections.title: JavaScript
sections.content:
- Analyze bundles (`@next/bundle-analyzer` or Turbopack's analyzer).
- Lazy-load heavy client components with `next/dynamic`.
- Enable the React Compiler.
- Use `optimizePackageImports` for icon/utility libraries.

sections.title: Measure
sections.content: Lighthouse, Vercel Speed Insights or `useReportWebVitals` for real-user metrics (LCP, INP, CLS).

codeExamples.title: Deferring a chat widget
codeExamples.explanation: The chat script loads during browser idle time, so it doesn't delay the page's main content or interactivity.

commonMistakes: Marking big layouts as client components.
Loading third-party scripts synchronously in the head.
realWorldExample: Teams improve INP by deferring analytics and chat scripts.
interviewTip: Structure the answer: rendering, assets, JavaScript, measurement.

quiz.prompt: Which next/script strategy loads a script during idle time?
quiz.explanation: lazyOnload waits for browser idle time.

title: Deploying Next.js
description: Options for running Next.js in production: managed platforms, Node servers, Docker and static export.

sections.title: Options
sections.content:
- **Managed platforms** (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare via OpenNext, AWS Amplify): zero-config, all features.
- **Node.js server:** `next build` then `next start` — supports all features.
- **Docker:** `output: 'standalone'` creates a minimal server bundle for containers.
- **Static export:** `output: 'export'` generates HTML files for any static host, but disables server features (Server Actions, dynamic rendering, cookies, image optimization defaults).

sections.title: Self-hosting considerations
sections.content: Configure a shared cache handler if you run multiple instances, put a CDN in front, and set `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` consistently across instances.

codeExamples.title: Standalone Docker build
codeExamples.explanation: The standalone output includes only the files needed to run, producing small container images.

commonMistakes: Using static export and then expecting Server Actions to work.
Running multiple instances without a shared cache.
realWorldExample: Companies run Next.js on Kubernetes with standalone output, or on Vercel with preview deployments per pull request.
interviewTip: Compare managed vs self-hosted trade-offs.

quiz.prompt: Server Actions work with output: 'export'.
quiz.explanation: Static export has no server runtime.

title: Runtimes: Node.js and Edge
description: Understand where your code runs and the trade-offs between runtimes.

sections.title: Node.js runtime
sections.content: The default for pages, Route Handlers and (in Next 16) proxy. Full Node.js APIs and npm compatibility.

sections.title: Edge runtime
sections.content: A lightweight runtime built on Web APIs that can start quickly close to users. It doesn't support all Node.js APIs (e.g. `fs`, many native modules), and some libraries won't work. Opt in per route with `export const runtime = 'edge'`.

sections.title: Choosing
sections.content: Default to Node.js. Consider edge for simple, latency-sensitive logic without heavy dependencies. Remember your database location often matters more than where the function runs.

codeExamples.title: Opting a route into the edge
codeExamples.explanation: A tiny, dependency-free handler is a good edge candidate. Heavy ORM queries are not.

commonMistakes: Running database-heavy code on the edge far from the database, increasing latency.
Using Node-only libraries on the edge runtime.
realWorldExample: Geolocation-based redirects and A/B bucketing are common edge workloads.
interviewTip: Mention that the database location usually dominates latency.

quiz.prompt: Which is the default runtime for Next.js route handlers?
quiz.explanation: Node.js is the default.

flashcards.front: How to opt a route into edge?

title: Security Best Practices
description: Protect data across Server Components, Actions and Route Handlers.

sections.title: Checklist
sections.content:
- Treat Server Actions and Route Handlers as public endpoints: authenticate, authorize, validate.
- Use a server-only Data Access Layer that returns DTOs.
- Never expose secrets via `NEXT_PUBLIC_`.
- Sanitize any HTML rendered with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.
- Set security headers (CSP, HSTS) and secure cookies.
- Rate-limit sensitive endpoints (login, sign-up).
- Keep Next.js and React updated — security patches ship regularly.

sections.title: Built-in protections
sections.content: Server Action ids are encrypted and unused actions are removed from the build; actions only accept POST with origin checks. React escapes rendered strings. These help, but don't replace your own checks.

codeExamples.title: Rate limiting a login action
codeExamples.explanation: Throttling by IP protects against brute-force attacks.

commonMistakes: Assuming page-level protection secures Server Actions on that page.
Logging sensitive data.
realWorldExample: After the 2025 middleware bypass advisory, teams audited apps that relied solely on middleware for auth.
interviewTip: Structure the answer around the DAL, validation, auth checks and headers.

quiz.prompt: If a page is protected, Server Actions defined in it are automatically protected.
quiz.explanation: Actions are separately callable endpoints.

title: Error Handling Strategy
description: Handle expected and unexpected errors consistently across the App Router.

sections.title: Expected errors
sections.content: Validation failures, 'not found', permission denied: return them from Server Actions (`{ error }`), call `notFound()`, or render a message. Don't throw.

sections.title: Unexpected errors
sections.content: Bugs and outages: let them throw and be caught by the nearest `error.tsx`. `global-error.tsx` covers the root layout.

sections.title: Reporting
sections.content: Export `onRequestError` from `instrumentation.ts` to report server errors (with request context) to your monitoring service.

codeExamples.title: Reporting server errors
codeExamples.explanation: Next.js calls `onRequestError` for errors during rendering, Route Handlers and Server Actions.

commonMistakes: Using try/catch around redirect() or notFound().
